Commands and output are generic examples. Kernel, image, package, and service versions affect specific behavior; check the documentation for the versions you use as you read.

Before modifying containers, images, mounts, or firewalls, back up Android data and stop the relevant sessions; examples involving deletion or forced stops may lose data. Manage NixOS system and user-environment configuration through Nix. The general Linux sections using apt/pacman, writing directly to /etc, or installing with pip do not apply to a NixOS host. Rebuild build, test, and switch operations and post-startup functional verification are separate stages.

The key to Waydroid performance is its GPU detection chain: it determines whether rendering uses hardware acceleration (GBM gralloc + Mesa EGL) or CPU software rendering (SwiftShader). Understanding the full chain, from scanning DRI nodes to mapping the Vulkan HAL and writing configuration files, is essential to choosing correctly between the hardware and software paths.
GPU detection

Waydroid’s GPU detection is implemented in tools/helpers/gpu.py, driven by the getDriNode() function. It does not depend on the running X11/Wayland environment; instead, it scans the Linux DRM subsystem directly to identify an available acceleration device before the container starts.
The DRM/DRI node model
The Linux kernel manages GPUs through the DRM (Direct Rendering Manager) subsystem. Each GPU exposes two types of character device:
Device node
Purpose
Example
modesetting — display-mode management (resolution, refresh rate, CRTC)
rendering — computation/rendering only (still subject to file permissions/ACLs, but does not require DRM master)

The key distinction: cardN requires DRM master privileges, usually held by the compositor, while renderDN can be opened for rendering/computation only by processes with the appropriate file permissions or ACLs. As an LXC container, Waydroid needs only a render node to participate in OpenGL/Vulkan acceleration, but still requires driver support in the image and appropriate authorization. It generally does not handle the host’s display modesetting; the host compositor (Wayland) handles display output.

The getDriNode() detection algorithm
The algorithm runs in five steps:
Step 1: check for a user override
Waydroid lets you specify a GPU device manually in /var/lib/waydroid/waydroid.cfg, under [waydroid]:

This is particularly useful on multi-GPU systems, such as laptops with an Intel iGPU + AMD dGPU. If automatic detection chooses the wrong GPU, specifying one manually bypasses the automatic scan order, but node-existence checks and driver filtering still apply.
Step 2: scan render nodes
Scan /dev/dri/renderD* in alphabetical order. Note that alphabetical order places renderD128 before renderD129, but does not guarantee that 128 corresponds to card0; verify the mapping through sysfs.
Step 3: read the kernel driver name
The driver name is read through sysfs rather than lspci, because sysfs provides a direct mapping from device nodes to kernel drivers without parsing the PCI topology.
Step 4: filter out NVIDIA

Modern NVIDIA drivers support GBM, but that does not guarantee compatibility between their userspace components and the Mesa/gralloc/EGL integration in Waydroid’s Android image. This upstream version still filters by the nvidia driver name. Nouveau appears in the mapping table; its performance and compatibility depend on the GPU generation, kernel, Mesa, and image, so it should not be declared universally unusable.
Step 5: obtain the corresponding card node
Look it up with getCardFromRender():

Determine which card node is associated with the render node. Although Waydroid does not use the card node directly for rendering, it needs their mapping to generate the complete LXC device-binding configuration.
The fallback path when no GPU is available
If getDriNode() returns None because there are no DRI nodes or all have been filtered out, make_base_props() automatically switches to software rendering:
This path is most common in VM environments, on NVIDIA platforms, and on servers without GPUs.
Vulkan driver mapping

After a DRI node is detected, getVulkanDriver() maps the kernel driver name to an Android Vulkan HAL implementation. The mapping logic is called in make_base_props(), and the generated properties are injected into waydroid_base.prop in the Android container.

Determining Intel GPU generations Intel is the only GPU vendor requiring an additional generation check. Waydroid reads /sys/kernel/debug/dri/0/i915_capabilities to obtain the GPU generation. When generation < 9, it uses intel_hasvk instead of intel. This is a separate Vulkan driver Mesa provides for older Intel GPUs and is incompatible with the newer intel Vulkan driver (ANV).
The make_base_props() configuration logic

make_base_props() also uses find_hidl() to check whether the android.hardware.graphics.allocator@4.0 HIDL service is available. If it is and a DRI node exists, hardware-accelerated configuration takes highest priority.

Only the render node selected by getDriNode() is mounted. Other render nodes on a multi-GPU system do not enter the container.
Switching between hardware acceleration and software rendering
GBM + Mesa EGL (the hardware-accelerated path)
This is Waydroid’s preferred path. It is enabled automatically when a DRI node is available:

GBM (Generic Buffer Management) is a userspace buffer-management API provided by Mesa and others that works with kernel DRM drivers. Waydroid’s GBM gralloc allocates Android graphics buffers through Mesa’s GBM backend. These buffers are allocated on the host GPU and can be used directly by the host compositor: zero-copy.
The process:
An Android app requests a graphics buffer
GBM gralloc allocates a BO (Buffer Object) on the host GPU through Mesa GBM
Android SurfaceFlinger passes the BO as a dma-buf
The Waydroid Session Manager converts the dma-buf to a Wayland wl_buffer
The compositor renders directly, with no CPU copy

Performance checks: compare the actual renderer, extensions, versions, and application workload. dma-buf can reduce copying, but cross-GPU operation and format/modifier mismatches can still cause copies or failures. It does not guarantee native-equivalent performance or a fixed API version.
SwiftShader (the software-rendering fallback)

SwiftShader is Google’s high-performance CPU renderer; specific API support depends on the build inside the container and its Android integration. It is not traditional slow software rendering: it uses JIT compilation and SIMD optimizations, but its performance gap relative to hardware acceleration must be measured for the workload.
When to use software rendering:
An optional fallback when the chosen NVIDIA path is incompatible with the image
A virtual machine without GPU passthrough (such as QEMU without virtio-gpu 3D)
A server without a GPU
A temporary fallback when hardware acceleration causes graphical problems

NVIDIA and hybrid-GPU compatibility options
The underlying problem with NVIDIA’s proprietary driver

Modern NVIDIA drivers support GBM. Waydroid’s limitation is integration across the entire Android graphics stack and driver; the explanation that “NVIDIA does not support GBM” is no longer valid. Waydroid’s hardware-acceleration stack is built entirely on GBM (GBM gralloc → Mesa EGL → dma-buf → Wayland), so getDriNode() has a hard-coded filter for NVIDIA’s proprietary driver.
This leaves NVIDIA users with three options:

NVIDIA and Wayland compositor alignment
Using the same GPU often reduces cross-device dma-buf compatibility problems, but it is not a universal strict requirement. Android-rendered buffers are exported to the compositor as dma-bufs; cross-device sharing depends on drivers, formats, and modifiers, and may fail, require a copy, or work normally. This means that even if the compositor runs on an NVIDIA GPU, you can first test a supported integrated GPU or software rendering and assess the compositor’s actual behavior.

AMD + AMD hybrid graphics
AMD APU + AMD dGPU systems, such as Ryzen + RX 6800M, are in a much better position than NVIDIA systems because both GPUs support GBM. However, there are known issues:
GitHub Issue #1454: on Ryzen 680M (APU) + RX 6800M (dGPU) systems, automatic detection may select the wrong GPU, causing Waydroid to enter a startup loop
Both GPUs also share the amdgpu kernel driver, and getDriNode()’s "return the first valid node" strategy may bind the container to a different GPU from the compositor

Solution: use drm_device to force selection of the same GPU as the compositor. AMD’s open-source Mesa drivers provide full GBM support for both GPUs; once the correct GPU is selected, functionality matches Intel’s.
Intel Arc discrete GPUs

Intel Arc (Alchemist/Battlemage) uses the i915 or xe kernel driver and is theoretically supported directly. However, the community currently reports unstable behavior: some Arc users experience graphical flickering or Vulkan initialization failures in Waydroid. The latest Mesa (24.1+) and a Linux 6.9+ kernel are recommended for the best support.
